title: Foreign keys
summary: An FK column stores the parent PK — the physical basis of relationships.

example.code: author_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES lab_authors(id)
example.sql: author_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES lab_authors(id)

exercise.prompt: Create lab_l04_publishers and lab_l04_magazines with publisher_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES lab_l04_publishers(id).
exercise.hint: REFERENCES parent(id) creates the FK constraint.

wrongSolutions.label: no REFERENCES
child created before the parent

body:
An FK column stores the parent PK — the physical basis of relationships.

Why it matters: Diagram lines and ORM relationship() / @relation are sugar over foreign keys. If the FK column (and constraint) is missing, joins and cascades have nothing to enforce.

SQL ↔ ORM: SQLAlchemy ForeignKey('lab_authors.id') ↔ Prisma fields/references ↔ SQL REFERENCES lab_authors(id).
why: Diagram lines and ORM relationship() / @relation are sugar over foreign keys. If the FK column (and constraint) is missing, joins and cascades have nothing to enforce.
objectives: Place the FK on the correct side (usually the 'many' / child).
Read FK errors as 'relationship not yet real in the database'.
pitfalls: Putting the FK on the parent for 1:N (backwards).
ORM relationship without an actual FK column — looks fine in code, fails the gate.
mappingNotes: SQLAlchemy ForeignKey('lab_authors.id') ↔ Prisma fields/references ↔ SQL REFERENCES lab_authors(id).
teachAlong: Cause: child row must belong to a parent.
Effect: child gets parent_id + FK constraint.
Diagram: arrow from child column to parent PK.
